cards.front: What is an internal threat?
cards.back: Someone inside with legitimate access (e.g. an employee) who sabotages, steals data or uses unauthorised software.

cards.front: What human factors cause accidental data loss?
cards.back: Negligence, poor training and not following security procedures.

cards.front: Name the named virus types in the spec.
cards.back: Boot sector, web script, macro, worm, rootkit, trojan, browser hijack, polymorphic.

cards.front: What is a polymorphic virus?
cards.back: A virus that changes its code each time it spreads, so signature-based antivirus misses it.

cards.front: What is spyware? Give an example.
cards.back: Software that secretly sends your data to a third party, e.g. a keylogger.

cards.front: What is ransomware and its main defence?
cards.back: Encrypts your files and demands payment. Defence: tested offline backups.

cards.front: What is a bot / botnet?
cards.back: Bot: an infected device under remote control. Botnet: many bots, used for spam or DDoS.

cards.front: Difference between DoS and DDoS?
cards.back: DoS: one machine floods a target. DDoS: many machines (a botnet), so it's harder to stop.

cards.front: Name the social engineering variants.
cards.back: Phishing (email), vishing (phone), smishing (SMS), whaling (execs), spear phishing (one person), pretexting, DNS spoofing.

cards.front: What is tailgating?
cards.back: Following an authorised person through a secure door without using your own credentials.

cards.front: Name the four types of impact of a cyber attack.
cards.back: Operational, financial, reputational and intellectual property loss.

cards.front: What is the NCSC?
cards.back: National Cyber Security Centre: the UK authority publishing current threat reports and advice.

cards.front: What is the OWASP Top 10?
cards.back: A regularly updated list of the most critical web app security risks, used in pen testing.

cards.front: Name the three firewall port categories.
cards.back: Well-known (e.g. 80 for HTTP), registered, and dynamic/private.

cards.front: What is a zero-day exploit?
cards.back: A new vulnerability with no patch yet, so attackers can exploit it first.

cards.front: What checks make a software download safe?
cards.back: Trusted source, HTTPS, a malware scan before installing, and a hash check.

cards.front: Give three IoT security risks.
cards.back: Default passwords, weak encryption and no security updates.

cards.front: Name vulnerability assessment tools.
cards.back: Port scanner, network mapper, registry checker and website vulnerability scanner.

cards.front: What is penetration testing?
cards.back: Authorised simulated attacks to find weak spots, ending in a report of findings.

cards.front: Name the three passive risk management measures.
cards.back: Transfer (e.g. insurance), avoidance (stop the activity) and acceptance.

cards.front: GDPR vs Computer Misuse Act — what does each cover?
cards.back: GDPR: personal data and privacy. CMA 1990: unauthorised access to or modification of computers.

cards.front: List key GDPR principles.
cards.back: Lawful, fair and transparent; set purpose; accurate; minimal data; kept minimum time; secure.

cards.front: Name GDPR personal rights.
cards.back: Access, be informed, correct/erase/restrict, object, portability, no solely automated decisions.

cards.front: Give examples of physical security measures.
cards.back: Locks, card entry, biometrics, CCTV, security staff and alarms.

cards.front: Name the three backup types.
cards.back: Full (everything), incremental (changes since last backup), differential (changes since last full).

cards.front: Signature scanning vs heuristics in antivirus?
cards.back: Signature: matches known malware. Heuristics: flags suspicious behaviour, catching new threats.

cards.front: Name the multi-factor authentication factor types.
cards.back: Knowledge (password), possession (USB key), inherence (fingerprint), plus location and behaviour.

cards.front: How does a USB security key work (MFA)?
cards.back: A possession factor: the system reads a code on the key to verify the user.

cards.front: Compare DAC, Role-Based and Rule-Based access control.
cards.back: DAC: owners control their files. Role-based: by job role. Rule-based: admin sets rules per user.

cards.front: Benefit and drawback of trusted computing?
cards.back: Benefit: an extra layer of security. Drawback: less user control and privacy.

cards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption?
cards.back: Symmetric: one shared key (AES), fast. Asymmetric: public/private pair (RSA), no shared secret.

cards.front: Why is MAC address filtering only 'medium' security?
cards.back: Only listed devices can join, but MAC addresses can be spoofed.

cards.front: What is an Evil Twin attack?
cards.back: A fake Wi-Fi access point copying a real one to intercept users' traffic.

cards.front: Name principles of secure system design.
cards.back: Expect attacks, least privilege, don't rely on secrecy, follow standards (ISO 27000).

cards.front: LAN vs WAN vs PAN?
cards.back: LAN: one site. WAN: large area (e.g. the internet). PAN: very short range (e.g. Bluetooth).

cards.front: Intranet vs extranet?
cards.back: Intranet: private, for staff. Extranet: gives selected outsiders (e.g. suppliers) controlled access.

cards.front: Client/server vs peer-to-peer?
cards.back: Client/server: a central server controls resources, easier to secure. P2P: devices share directly.

cards.front: How does virtualisation improve security?
cards.back: It isolates risky processes (sandboxing/containers), shrinking the attack surface.

cards.front: Give security issues with BYOD.
cards.back: Company data on personal devices, enforcing passwords, patching, and wiping data when staff leave.

cards.front: Security issues of remote working?
cards.back: Insecure home Wi-Fi, family using devices, third-party tools. Needs a VPN.

cards.front: Switch vs router vs gateway?
cards.back: Switch: links devices in a LAN. Router: links networks. Gateway: translates between protocols.

cards.front: Security issues of external media?
cards.back: Loss/theft, interception, failure and malware. Mitigate with encryption.

cards.front: What is TCP/IP?
cards.back: The core rules for sending data across networks as packets, with error correction.

cards.front: What are the parts of a packet?
cards.back: Header (addresses, control info), payload (the data), trailer (error checking).

cards.front: TCP vs UDP?
cards.back: TCP: reliable, resends lost packets (files/web). UDP: faster, no guarantee (streaming/VoIP).

cards.front: What is NAT?
cards.back: Maps private IPs to one public IP, hiding the internal network.

cards.front: Name the RFC 1918 private IP ranges.
Security benefits of network segmentation?
cards.back: Limits access, stops attackers moving sideways, and shrinks the attack surface.

cards.front: Which device gives secure internet access on a network diagram?
cards.back: A firewall, between the router and the internal network.

cards.front: What does DNS do?
cards.back: Turns domain names (e.g. example.com) into IP addresses.

cards.front: What is DHCP and why is it insecure?
cards.back: Automatically assigns IP settings. No built-in security, so a rogue DHCP server can be set up.

cards.front: Name pieces of DHCP configuration information.
cards.back: IP range, reserved IPs, lease length, default gateway and server address.

cards.front: How does a VPN work?
cards.back: An encrypted tunnel over the internet, so intercepted data can't be read.

cards.front: Why are SMTP/POP email protocols a security weakness?
cards.back: No built-in encryption, so emails can be read in transit unless TLS is added.

cards.front: Physical vs logical topology?
cards.back: Physical: the actual layout of devices and cables. Logical: how data flows.

cards.front: What is a packet sniffer used for?
cards.back: Captures and inspects traffic: for troubleshooting, or by attackers to eavesdrop.

cards.front: What is the Plan-Do-Check-Act loop?
cards.back: A repeating improvement cycle from ISO 27001, because threats keep changing.

cards.front: What should a password policy contain?
cards.back: Length/complexity, no sharing, no reuse, expiry, lockout, and banned common passwords.

cards.front: Features of effective staff security training?
cards.back: Management-funded, flexible, varied, tracked, incentivised and ongoing.

cards.front: What is a security audit?
cards.back: A check that the organisation meets its policies and the law, reporting gaps to fix.

cards.front: What should a backup policy include?
cards.back: What data, method/type, frequency, storage, who's responsible, and testing.

cards.front: Stages of a cyber security incident response?
cards.back: Triage/escalation → response (contain, mitigate, recover) → review and close.

cards.front: Who should be on an incident response contact list?
cards.back: Incident lead, IT lead, senior management, legal, PR, HR and insurance.

cards.front: What is triage in a disaster recovery policy?
cards.back: List possible events, rate their severity, and choose the response (incident, BCP or full DR).

cards.front: What does an external services policy cover?
cards.back: Rules for outside providers: who authorises, who's accountable, SLAs and incident handling.

cards.front: Key elements of a data protection policy?
cards.back: A Data Protection Officer, GDPR principles, staff training, and covering contractors.

cards.front: Why use a Faraday bag/cage when seizing a device?
cards.back: It blocks wireless signals so the device can't be remotely wiped.

cards.front: What is chain of custody?
cards.back: A record of everyone who handled the evidence, proving it wasn't tampered with.

cards.front: Why is live forensics challenging?
cards.back: RAM is lost at power-off, data keeps changing, and remote data is hard to capture.

cards.front: What are contemporaneous notes?
cards.back: Notes made at the time, making evidence more reliable and admissible.

cards.front: Physical image vs targeted image of a drive?
cards.back: Physical: the whole drive, including deleted files. Targeted: selected files only, may miss evidence.

cards.front: Why generate a hash/checksum of a forensic image?
cards.back: To prove the copy matches the original and hasn't been altered.

cards.front: Why work from a copy/image, not the original device?
cards.back: Changing the original could make it inadmissible, so you work on a copy.

cards.front: What is 'alert fatigue'?
cards.back: So many (often false) alerts that investigators stop noticing real ones.

cards.front: Name signs that a system has been compromised.
cards.back: Unusual traffic, logins, DNS requests or port use, and odd file reads or changes.

cards.front: What should a security report contain?
cards.back: A clear structure, what went wrong, and recommended improvements.

cards.front: What must you do before network forensic scanning?
cards.back: Agree a method, get permission, and make sure it won't disrupt the live system.

cards.front: Steps to isolate a seized device from networks?
cards.back: Photograph the screen, then cut its connections (power off, airplane mode, Faraday bag).
